title: Cache Coherence
summary: Multiple cores, multiple caches, one memory. Learn why copies go stale, how MESI keeps them honest, and why false sharing quietly kills performance.

blocks.markdown:
**Cache coherence** is the guarantee that every core's private cache agrees on the value of shared memory, even though each has its own copy.

- On a multicore chip, each core has its own [cache-fundamentals](cache-fundamentals) cache.
- If one core writes and others still hold the old copy, they see **stale data**.
- A coherence protocol fixes this automatically, in hardware, so software doesn't have to.
- See [multicore-multiprocessing](multicore-multiprocessing) for the bigger picture.

Say variable `x = 0` sits in main memory, and cores A and B both cache it.

- Core A writes `x = 5` — but only its own cached copy changes at first.
- Core B still has `x = 0` cached and keeps reading the stale value.
- Without coordination, two cores can now disagree about the same memory location.

Coherence exists purely to stop this.

Two different guarantees, often confused.

- **Coherence** — all cores see a **single, up-to-date value** for one memory location.
- **Consistency** — the **order** in which changes to different locations become visible across cores.

Coherence is per-address; consistency is about ordering across addresses. See [memory-consistency-models](memory-consistency-models).

blocks.subTitle: Write-invalidate vs write-update
blocks.markdown:
Two strategies for handling a write to shared data.

| Approach | On a write |
|---|---|
| Write-invalidate | Other copies are marked invalid; they reload on next use |
| Write-update | Other copies are refreshed with the new value immediately |

Write-invalidate wins in practice — one small invalidate message uses far less bus traffic than broadcasting full data on every write.

blocks.subTitle: Snooping
blocks.markdown:
**Snooping** is when every core's cache controller watches a shared bus and notices memory traffic from other cores.

- All caches see every read/write broadcast on the bus.
- If a core sees another core write to an address it holds, it invalidates its own copy.
- Simple and fast for a **small number of cores**, but the shared bus becomes a bottleneck as core count grows.

blocks.subTitle: Directory-based
blocks.markdown:
**Directory-based coherence** keeps a central **directory** that tracks which cores hold a copy of each cache line.

- A write looks up the directory and sends invalidations only to the cores that actually have a copy.
- No broadcast to everyone, so it scales to **many cores** — used in large multiprocessors.
- Cost: extra memory for the directory and a lookup step on every access.

blocks.subTitle: Snooping vs directory
blocks.markdown:
The tradeoff in one line: broadcast-and-simple vs tracked-and-scalable.

| | Snooping | Directory |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanism | Broadcast on shared bus | Central directory per line |
| Scales to | Few cores | Many cores |

Small multicore chips snoop; large multiprocessors need a directory.

blocks.subTitle: The four states
blocks.markdown:
**MESI** is the most common write-invalidate protocol. Every cache line is tagged with one of four states.

- **Modified (M)** — dirty, changed here only; this cache must write it back eventually.
- **Exclusive (E)** — clean, only this cache has it; safe to write without asking anyone.
- **Shared (S)** — clean, other caches may also have this line.
- **Invalid (I)** — this copy is unusable; must fetch before reading.

blocks.subTitle: Why Exclusive matters
blocks.markdown:
Exclusive exists purely as an optimization over a simpler 3-state (Modified/Shared/Invalid) protocol.

- Without it, every write needs a bus message to check if anyone else has the line — even when nobody does.
- With **Exclusive**, a core that reads a line no one else has can later write it **silently**, no bus traffic.
- Common case: one thread's private data. E saves messages exactly there.

blocks.subTitle: What it is
blocks.markdown:
**False sharing** is when two unrelated variables happen to sit in the **same cache line**, so cores editing different variables still fight over the line.

- Core A writes `counterA`, Core B writes `counterB` — different variables, same 64-byte line.
- Each write invalidates the other core's copy of the *whole line*, forcing a reload.
- The line ping-pongs between caches even though the cores never touch each other's data.

blocks.subTitle: Why it hurts
blocks.markdown:
False sharing looks like a race condition in profilers but isn't one — the code is correct, just slow.

- Every ping-pong costs a coherence round trip, hundreds of cycles, instead of a cheap cache hit.
- More cores hammering the same line makes it worse, not better — this is why some code doesn't scale.
- It's a **performance bug only**; results stay correct.

blocks.subTitle: Avoiding it

blocks.markdown:
Common mix-ups:

- **"Coherence means my program is race-free."** No — coherence keeps one address consistent; it says nothing about the order of operations across addresses (that's consistency).
- **"More cores always means more bus traffic with snooping."** True, which is exactly why big systems switch to directories.
- **"False sharing is a correctness bug."** It isn't — only performance suffers.

blocks.subTitle: What problem does coherence solve
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What problem does cache coherence solve?**

On a multicore chip each core has its own cache, so the same memory location can live in several places at once. If one core writes and others still hold the old value, they silently read stale data. A coherence protocol makes writes visible to every cache automatically, so all cores agree on the current value.

blocks.subTitle: Explain MESI
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Walk me through the MESI protocol.**

Each cache line is Modified (dirty, only here), Exclusive (clean, only here), Shared (clean, others may have it), or Invalid (unusable). A local write moves a line to Modified and invalidates every other copy; a read on a line no one else has grabs Exclusive; if others already have it, everyone lands in Shared. Any outside write flips a cached copy to Invalid.

blocks.subTitle: Snooping vs directory
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Snooping vs directory-based coherence — when would you use each?**

Snooping has every cache watch a shared bus and react to broadcasts — simple, low latency, but the bus saturates as core count grows. Directory-based coherence tracks sharers per line centrally and messages only the cores that need it — more overhead per access, but it scales to large multiprocessors where broadcast isn't feasible.

blocks.subTitle: False sharing and fixes
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is false sharing and how do you avoid it?**

It's when two variables used by different cores happen to sit in the same cache line, so unrelated writes keep invalidating each other's copy of that line — a pure performance problem, not a correctness one. Fix by padding or aligning hot variables so each lands on its own cache line.

blocks.subTitle: Coherence vs consistency
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What's the difference between cache coherence and memory consistency?**

Coherence guarantees all cores eventually see the same value for a single address. Consistency defines the rules for the order in which writes to different addresses become visible to other cores. You can have perfect coherence and still get surprising results if the consistency model allows reordering.

blocks.subTitle: Write-invalidate vs write-update
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why do most real protocols use write-invalidate instead of write-update?**

Write-update has to broadcast the new data to every sharer on every single write, which floods the bus. Write-invalidate sends one small invalidate message and lets other cores reload lazily only if they actually read the line again — far less traffic in practice, so it's what MESI and its variants use.
